title: Why I made Basil shared
summary: A founder explanation of why Basil begins in one shared Community Garden instead of a separate private world for every player.
whyToday: This is the clearest introduction to Basil's central difference: a calm garden where one person's care can become part of somebody else's return visit.
hook: Most gardening games give you a world of your own.
narration: Most gardening games give you a world of your own. I wanted Basil to begin with the opposite idea. Everyone enters the same living garden. You can plant a flower, leave, and somebody you have never met may come along and water it. Their care changes what you return to. That is the whole experiment behind Basil: what happens when progress means leaving a shared place a little better than you found it?
sourceNote: Founder commentary grounded in Basil's actual shared Community Garden and watering mechanics.
outroLine: Plant something for the next person.

youtube.headline: Why I made a gardening game shared by everyone
youtube.body: Most gardening games give you a world of your own. Basil starts with the opposite idea: one shared garden, where a flower you plant can be watered by someone you have never met. Plant one free in your browser.

instagram.headline: What if a gardening game belonged to everyone?
instagram.body: I made Basil around one small experiment: plant something, leave, and return to a garden another person may have cared for. It is calm, shared, and playable in your browser.

reddit.headline: I made a gardening game where everyone enters the same garden
reddit.body: Most gardening games begin by giving each player a private world. I wanted to try the opposite with Basil: one shared Community Garden where you can plant a flower and somebody else may later water it. I am curious whether shared progress makes a peaceful game feel more meaningful. What would make you want to return to a garden like this?
